records.source: Μετὰ δὲ πέντε ἡμέρας κατέβη ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς Ἁνανίας μετὰ πρεσβυτέρων τινῶν καὶ ῥήτορος Τερτύλλου τινός, οἵτινες ἐνεφάνισαν τῷ ἡγεμόνι κατὰ τοῦ Παύλου.
records.gloss: After then five days came down the high priest Ananias with elders some and an orator Tertullus a certain, who made a representation to the governor against Paul.
pieces: Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some of the elders and a trained advocate named Tertullus, and they laid out their case against Paul before the governor.

L.1: And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a certain orator, Tertullus, who brought charges before the governor against Paul.

R.1: Five days later, Ananias the high priest came down to Caesarea. Some of the Jewish elders came with him, and so did a lawyer named Tertullus. They told the governor what charges they had against Paul.

decisions.choice: the high priest Ananias: the same man who had Paul struck in the council (23:2)
decisions.reason: Ananias son of Nedebaeus was high priest at this time; Josephus tells of his wealth and violence (Antiquities 20.205-207). He came in person to press the case.

decisions.choice: orator: a trained public speaker who argued cases in court, an advocate
decisions.reason: The word names a man skilled in public speech. Here he speaks for the prosecution before a Roman governor, as an advocate would. His speech in 24:2-8 follows the forms of a court speech.

decisions.choice: brought charges: laid formal information before an official
decisions.reason: The verb means to make something known to an authority. Here, as in 25:2 and 25:15, it is used of a formal accusation in court.

decisions.choice: after five days: counted from Paul's arrival in Caesarea, or from his departure from Jerusalem
alternatives: after five days of the trial
decisions.reason: Luke does not say where the count starts. Felix had promised a hearing when the accusers arrived (23:35); this is that hearing.

decisions.choice: came down to Caesarea; Jewish elders
decisions.reason: Readable names the place, Caesarea, where Paul was held (23:33), and says whose elders these were.

decisions.choice: a trained advocate; a lawyer
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "orator". Balanced and Readable say what he did here: he argued the case in court.

records.heading: Tertullus brings the case against Paul

records.source: κληθέντος δὲ αὐτοῦ ἤρξατο κατηγορεῖν ὁ Τέρτυλλος λέγων· Πολλῆς εἰρήνης τυγχάνοντες διὰ σοῦ καὶ διορθωμάτων γινομένων τῷ ἔθνει τούτῳ διὰ τῆς σῆς προνοίας πάντῃ τε καὶ πανταχοῦ ἀποδεχόμεθα, κράτιστε Φῆλιξ, μετὰ πάσης εὐχαριστίας.
records.gloss: Having been called then of him began to accuse Tertullus saying, Great peace we are attaining through you and reforms are being done to the nation this through your foresight, \v 3 in every way both and everywhere we gladly accept [it], most excellent Felix, with all thankfulness.
pieces: When Paul had been called in, Tertullus opened the prosecution: "Thanks to you we live in great peace, and your careful planning has set many things right for this nation.
Most excellent Felix, we welcome all this in every way and in every place, with heartfelt thanks.

L.2: And when he had been called, Tertullus began to accuse [him], saying, "Since through you we enjoy much peace, and reforms are coming about for this nation through your foresight,
L.3: in every way and everywhere we welcome [it], most excellent Felix, with all gratitude.

R.2: Paul was called in, and Tertullus began to accuse him. He said, "Because of you, we have had a long time of peace. Your wise plans have made many things better for our nation.
R.3: Most excellent Felix, we are thankful for this everywhere and in every way.

decisions.choice: a flattering opening: praise of the judge, as court speeches customarily began
decisions.reason: Speeches to a judge usually began by winning his goodwill. Felix's rule was in fact remembered as harsh: the Roman historian Tacitus says he used a king's power with the mind of a slave (Histories 5.9), and Josephus tells of the unrest under him (Antiquities 20.160-181). Paul's own opening in 24:10 is much more restrained.

decisions.choice: reforms: improvements, things set right
decisions.reason: The word means a setting straight. Tertullus credits Felix with measures that improved life for the nation.

decisions.choice: foresight: careful planning ahead
decisions.reason: The word means forethought. Applied to a ruler it praises his wise provision for his subjects.

decisions.choice: most excellent: a formal title for a high Roman official
decisions.reason: The same title is used for Felix in the commander's letter (23:26) and for Festus (26:25). It was the customary address for men of the equestrian order who held office.

decisions.choice: when he had been called: Paul
decisions.reason: Paul was held in Herod's palace (23:35) and was summoned for the hearing.

decisions.choice: Paul
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the man who was called in.

records.source: ἵνα δὲ μὴ ἐπὶ πλεῖόν σε ἐγκόπτω, παρακαλῶ ἀκοῦσαί σε ἡμῶν συντόμως τῇ σῇ ἐπιεικείᾳ.
records.gloss: In order that however not any longer you I should be a hindrance, I implore to hear you us briefly in your kindness.
pieces: But I do not want to keep you long, so I ask you, in your fairness, to give us a brief hearing.

L.4: But so that I may not detain you any further, I beg you to hear us briefly in your graciousness.

R.4: I do not want to take up too much of your time. Please be patient with us and listen for a short time.

decisions.choice: detain you: hold you up, take more of your time
decisions.reason: The verb means to cut in or hinder. Tertullus promises to be short, a common courtesy in court speeches.

decisions.choice: graciousness: a ruler's fairness and forbearance
decisions.reason: The word describes reasonable, considerate conduct, the opposite of harshness (compare 2 Corinthians 10:1). Tertullus flatters Felix again.

decisions.choice: be patient with us
decisions.reason: Readable puts the appeal to Felix's forbearance in plain words.

records.source: εὑρόντες γὰρ τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον λοιμὸν καὶ κινοῦντα στάσεις πᾶσι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις τοῖς κατὰ τὴν οἰκουμένην πρωτοστάτην τε τῆς τῶν Ναζωραίων αἱρέσεως, ὃς καὶ τὸ ἱερὸν ἐπείρασεν βεβηλῶσαι, ὃν καὶ ἐκρατήσαμεν, παρ’ οὗ δυνήσῃ αὐτὸς ἀνακρίνας περὶ πάντων τούτων ἐπιγνῶναι ὧν ἡμεῖς κατηγοροῦμεν αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Having found for the man this a pest and stirring insurrections among all the Jews in the world, a ringleader then of the of the Nazarenes sect, \v 6 who even the temple attempted to profane, whom also we seized, \v 8 from whom you will be able yourself having examined concerning all these things to know of which we accuse him.
pieces: This man, we have found, is a public menace. He causes unrest among the Jews in every part of the world, and he is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.
He even attempted to defile the temple, and we took hold of him.
Question him yourself, and you will learn from him all about the things we accuse him of."

L.5: For we have found this man a plague, and one stirring up riots among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes,
L.6: who even tried to profane the temple, whom we also seized.
L.8: By examining him yourself you will be able to learn from him about all these things of which we accuse him."

R.5: This man is a troublemaker. All over the world he stirs up trouble among the Jews. He is a leader of the group called the Nazarenes.
R.6: He even tried to make the temple unclean, so we arrested him.
R.8: Ask him questions yourself. Then you will find out about all the things we accuse him of."

decisions.choice: a plague: a public danger, a pest
decisions.reason: The word means a pestilence. Used of a person, it calls him a danger to the community, a menace.

decisions.choice: stirring up riots: causing civil unrest
decisions.reason: The word means uprisings or riots (compare 19:40; 23:10). Before a Roman governor this was the most serious charge, since Rome punished any threat to public order.

decisions.choice: sect: a party or school within Judaism
decisions.reason: The word is used of the Sadducees (5:17) and the Pharisees (15:5; 26:5). It names a group, not yet a false teaching. Paul takes up the word in 24:14.

decisions.choice: the Nazarenes: the followers of Jesus of Nazareth
decisions.reason: Only here in the New Testament are the believers called by this name. Jesus is "the Nazarene" in 2:22, 3:6 and 22:8.

decisions.choice: profane the temple: make it unclean, treat it as common
decisions.reason: The charge goes back to 21:28, where Paul was accused of bringing Greeks into the temple.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: the sentence goes on from "we seized" to "from him"; verse 7 is not in the text
alternatives: many manuscripts add 6b-8a: "and we wanted to judge him by our law. But the commander Lysias came and with great force took him out of our hands, ordering his accusers to come before you"
decisions.reason: The longer reading is found in many later manuscripts and was followed by the King James Version; it is missing from the oldest manuscripts. That is why most editions have no verse 7 here. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: from him: from Paul, by examining him
decisions.reason: In the SBLGNT the nearest person is Paul. In the longer text (see the variant) the words would point to Lysias.

decisions.choice: a public menace; a troublemaker
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the picture; Balanced and Readable say what it means of a person.

decisions.choice: make the temple unclean
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what defiling the temple meant.

records.source: συνεπέθεντο δὲ καὶ οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι φάσκοντες ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχειν.
records.gloss: Joined in the attack then also the Jews, declaring these things so to be.
pieces: The Jews who had come added their voices, claiming that it was all so.

L.9: And the Jews also joined in the attack, asserting that these things were so.

R.9: The Jews who were there agreed with Tertullus. They said that all of it was true.

decisions.choice: joined in the attack: joined in pressing the charge
decisions.reason: The verb means to join in attacking someone. Here the others took up the accusation with Tertullus.

decisions.choice: the Jews who had come; who were there
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that these are the high priest and elders of 24:1.

records.source: Ἀπεκρίθη τε ὁ Παῦλος νεύσαντος αὐτῷ τοῦ ἡγεμόνος λέγειν· Ἐκ πολλῶν ἐτῶν ὄντα σε κριτὴν τῷ ἔθνει τούτῳ ἐπιστάμενος εὐθύμως τὰ περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ ἀπολογοῦμαι, δυναμένου σου ἐπιγνῶναι, ὅτι οὐ πλείους εἰσίν μοι ἡμέραι δώδεκα ἀφ’ ἧς ἀνέβην προσκυνήσων εἰς Ἰερουσαλήμ, καὶ οὔτε ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ εὗρόν με πρός τινα διαλεγόμενον ἢ ἐπίστασιν ποιοῦντα ὄχλου οὔτε ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς οὔτε κατὰ τὴν πόλιν, οὐδὲ παραστῆσαι δύνανταί σοι περὶ ὧν νυνὶ κατηγοροῦσίν μου.
records.gloss: Answered then Paul, having nodded to him the governor to speak, For many years being you judge to the nation this knowing, cheerfully the things concerning myself I make a defense, \v 11 being able you to know that not more there are to me days twelve from which I went up to worship in Jerusalem, \v 12 and neither in the temple did they find me with anyone reasoning or a gathering making of a crowd, nor in the synagogues nor in the city, \v 13 nor to prove to you are they able concerning [the things] of which now they accuse me.
pieces: The governor signaled to Paul to speak, and he answered: "You have judged this nation for many years, and knowing that, I am glad to answer for myself before you.
It is only twelve days, no more, since I went up to Jerusalem to worship, as you can find out.
They never found me in the temple in debate with anyone or drawing a crowd together, nor in the synagogues, nor anywhere in the city.
They have no proof to set before you for the things they now charge me with.

L.10: And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul answered, "Knowing that for many years you have been a judge to this nation, I cheerfully make my defense concerning myself,
L.11: since you are able to learn that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem.
L.12: And neither in the temple did they find me arguing with anyone or causing a crowd to gather, nor in the synagogues, nor in the city.
L.13: Nor are they able to prove to you the things of which they now accuse me.

R.10: Then the governor nodded to Paul, to show that he could speak. Paul said, "You have been a judge over this nation for many years. So I am glad to speak to you and defend myself.
R.11: You can check this for yourself: only twelve days ago I went up to Jerusalem to worship God.
R.12: These people did not find me arguing with anyone in the temple. They did not see me stirring up a crowd in the synagogues or anywhere else in the city.
R.13: They cannot prove any of the things they say against me.

decisions.choice: Paul's opening: a courteous but plain appeal to the judge's experience
decisions.reason: Paul also opens by addressing the judge, as court speeches did, but he praises nothing. He only says that Felix has long experience of the Jewish nation and so can judge these matters. Felix had governed Judea for some years by now.

decisions.choice: not more than twelve days: since Paul arrived in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Counting from his arrival (21:17), Paul had spent only a few days in the city before his arrest. The short time makes the charge of stirring up riots across the world look unlikely.

decisions.choice: arguing: discussing, debating
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used of Paul's discussions in synagogues (17:2; 18:4; 19:8). He says he did not even do that in Jerusalem this time.

decisions.choice: causing a crowd to gather: stirring up a mob
decisions.reason: The noun means a gathering together, here of a crowd. Paul answers the charge of 24:5 directly.

decisions.choice: prove: set out evidence for
decisions.reason: The verb means to present or establish. The accusers bring charges but no proof.

decisions.choice: to worship God
decisions.reason: Readable names the one Paul came to worship.

decisions.choice: It is only twelve days ... as you can find out
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the fact first and the appeal to Felix's knowledge after it, to make a shorter English sentence.

records.heading: Paul makes his defense before Felix

records.source: ὁμολογῶ δὲ τοῦτό σοι ὅτι κατὰ τὴν ὁδὸν ἣν λέγουσιν αἵρεσιν οὕτως λατρεύω τῷ πατρῴῳ θεῷ, πιστεύων πᾶσι τοῖς κατὰ τὸν νόμον καὶ τοῖς ἐν τοῖς προφήταις γεγραμμένοις, ἐλπίδα ἔχων εἰς τὸν θεόν, ἣν καὶ αὐτοὶ οὗτοι προσδέχονται, ἀνάστασιν μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι δικαίων τε καὶ ἀδίκων·
records.gloss: I confess however this to you, that according to the Way which they call a sect, so I serve the ancestral God, believing all things according to the law and that in the Prophets have been written, \v 15 a hope having toward God, which also these themselves await, a resurrection to be about to be of both righteous and unrighteous.
pieces: This much I do acknowledge before you: it is as one who follows the Way, which they call a sect, that I serve the God of our {{gender:ancestors|fathers}}. I believe all that accords with the law and all that stands written in the Prophets.
My hope rests on God, and these men look for it too: that a resurrection is coming, of the righteous and the unrighteous alike.

L.14: But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, so I serve the God of [our] fathers, believing everything that accords with the law and that is written in the Prophets,
L.15: having a hope in God, which these men themselves also await, that there is going to be a resurrection of both [the] righteous and [the] unrighteous.

R.14: But I will tell you this. I follow the Way. They call it a sect, but in this Way I worship the God of our {{gender:ancestors|fathers}}. I believe everything that the law says and everything that is written in the books of the prophets.
R.15: I trust God, and I have the same hope these men have: God will raise the dead to life, both those who did right and those who did wrong.

decisions.choice: the Way: the movement of those who follow Jesus
alternatives: a way of life in general
decisions.reason: Luke uses this name for the believers in 9:2, 19:9, 19:23 and 22:4. Paul uses it in place of the word his accusers chose.

decisions.choice: a sect: a party that splits off
decisions.reason: Tertullus used the word in 24:5. Paul does not accept it as a fair name: he worships the same God and holds the same Scriptures. The word could be neutral (26:5), but here it is the accusers' label.

decisions.choice: serve: worship God with religious service
decisions.reason: The verb is used of worship and service given to God (7:7; 26:7; 27:23).

decisions.choice: the God of our fathers: the God of Israel's forebears
decisions.reason: The adjective means inherited from the fathers. Paul claims continuity with Israel's faith (compare 3:13; 5:30; 22:14).

decisions.choice: the law and the Prophets: the Scriptures of Israel
decisions.reason: The law and the Prophets were two parts of the Hebrew Scriptures, and the phrase stands for the whole (13:15; 28:23).

decisions.choice: a resurrection of the righteous and the unrighteous: all the dead will be raised for judgment
decisions.reason: Daniel 12:2 speaks of many rising, some to life and some to shame, and Jesus says the same in John 5:28-29. The word for righteous here is the adjective for people who are just, not the noun righteousness in 24:25.

decisions.choice: which these men themselves also await: the hope held by Paul's Jewish accusers
decisions.reason: Many Jews, the Pharisees above all, hoped for the resurrection (23:6-8). The Sadducees denied it, so Paul speaks of what his people hold in general, not of every person present.

decisions.choice: those who did right and those who did wrong
decisions.reason: Readable explains the two groups in plain words.

decisions.choice: God will raise the dead to life
alternatives: a resurrection is going to be
decisions.reason: Readable says what the resurrection is and who brings it about.

records.source: ἐν τούτῳ καὶ αὐτὸς ἀσκῶ ἀπρόσκοπον συνείδησιν ἔχειν πρὸς τὸν θεὸν καὶ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους διὰ παντός.
records.gloss: In this also I myself strive without offense a conscience to have toward God and men through everything.
pieces: That is why I, for my part, take pains to live with a blameless conscience toward God and toward people at all times.

L.16: In this I myself also strive always to have a conscience without offense toward God and {{gender:people|men}}.

R.16: Because of this hope, I always try hard to do what is right before God and before people. Then my conscience does not blame me for anything.

decisions.choice: in this: because of this hope
decisions.reason: The phrase most likely looks back to the hope of the resurrection and the judgment it brings. It could also mean "meanwhile" or "in this way of life".

decisions.choice: a conscience without offense: one that has nothing to accuse
alternatives: a conscience that causes no one to stumble
decisions.reason: The adjective means not stumbling or not giving offense. Paul says something similar before the council in 23:1.

decisions.choice: because of this hope
decisions.reason: Readable says what "this" refers to, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: try hard to do what is right ... my conscience does not blame me
alternatives: strive to have a conscience without offense
decisions.reason: Readable explains what a clear conscience means in two short sentences.

records.source: δι’ ἐτῶν δὲ πλειόνων ἐλεημοσύνας ποιήσων εἰς τὸ ἔθνος μου παρεγενόμην καὶ προσφοράς, ἐν αἷς εὗρόν με ἡγνισμένον ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ, οὐ μετὰ ὄχλου οὐδὲ μετὰ θορύβου, τινὲς δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀσίας Ἰουδαῖοι, οὓς ἔδει ἐπὶ σοῦ παρεῖναι καὶ κατηγορεῖν εἴ τι ἔχοιεν πρὸς ἐμέ, ἢ αὐτοὶ οὗτοι εἰπάτωσαν τί εὗρον ἀδίκημα στάντος μου ἐπὶ τοῦ συνεδρίου ἢ περὶ μιᾶς ταύτης φωνῆς ἧς ἐκέκραξα ἐν αὐτοῖς ἑστὼς ὅτι Περὶ ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν ἐγὼ κρίνομαι σήμερον ἐφ’ ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: After years now several alms to bring to the nation of me I arrived and offerings, \v 18 in which they found me purified in the temple, not with a crowd nor with tumult, \v 19 some however from Asia Jews, who ought before you to be present and to accuse, if anything they may have against me; \v 20 or these themselves let them say what they found wrongdoing, having stood me before the council, \v 21 or concerning one this voice which I cried out among them standing, that Concerning resurrection of dead I am judged today by you.
pieces: I had been away for a number of years, and I came to bring charitable gifts to my people and to make offerings.
I was doing this when they found me in the temple, ritually purified, with no crowd around me and no disorder.
But some Jews from Asia were the ones who saw me. They should have come before you to accuse me, if they have any complaint against me.
Otherwise, let the men who are here tell you what wrong they discovered in me when I stood before the council,
unless it was the one sentence I called out as I stood among them: 'I am being judged by you today over the resurrection of the dead.'"

L.17: Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation, and offerings,
L.18: in the course of which they found me purified in the temple, not with a crowd nor with an uproar.
L.19: But [there were] some Jews from Asia, who ought to be present before you and to accuse [me], if they should have anything against me.
L.20: Or let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council,
L.21: other than about this one statement which I cried out while standing among them: 'Concerning [the] resurrection of [the] dead I am being judged today by you.'"

R.17: I had been away from Jerusalem for several years. Then I came back to bring money to help the poor among my people, and to offer gifts to God.
R.18: I was doing this when they found me in the temple. I had gone through the ceremony to make myself clean. There was no crowd with me, and I was not causing any trouble.
R.19: But some Jews from the province of Asia were there. They are the ones who should be here in front of you. If they have something against me, they should say so.
R.20: Or let these men who are here say what wrong I did when I stood in front of their council.
R.21: The only thing I did was call out one sentence while I stood there. I said, 'You are judging me today because I believe that the dead will rise.'"

decisions.choice: alms to my nation: gifts for the poor among the Jewish people
decisions.reason: Paul's letters tell of a collection he gathered from the churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25-28; 1 Corinthians 16:1-4; 2 Corinthians 8-9). This is probably what he means, the only mention of it in Acts. Before Felix he calls it simply alms for his nation.

decisions.choice: offerings: sacrifices presented in the temple
decisions.reason: The word is used of sacrifices. It may refer to the offerings for the vow in 21:23-26.

decisions.choice: purified: having gone through the rites of purification
decisions.reason: Paul had purified himself with four men under a vow before entering the temple (21:24, 21:26). So he was not defiling the temple, as the charge in 24:6 claimed.

decisions.choice: But some Jews from Asia: Paul breaks off his sentence
decisions.reason: The Greek begins a new subject and does not finish the clause about what these Jews did; it moves straight to where they should be now. Literal keeps the broken shape with supplied words.

decisions.choice: who ought to be present before you: the first accusers are missing
alternatives: they were not allowed to come
decisions.reason: The Jews from Asia started the riot (21:27). Roman practice expected accusers to face the accused in person (compare 25:16), and they had not come.

decisions.choice: the council: the Jewish high council in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: This is the council of chief priests, elders and scribes before which Paul stood in 23:1-10.

decisions.choice: this one statement: Paul's cry in the council
decisions.reason: Paul quotes his own words in 23:6, which set the Pharisees and Sadducees against each other.

decisions.choice: charitable gifts
decisions.reason: "Alms" is old-fashioned; Balanced says what they were.

decisions.choice: because I believe that the dead will rise
alternatives: concerning the resurrection of the dead
decisions.reason: Readable says what the question about the resurrection was: whether the dead will rise, which Paul believed.

records.source: Ἀνεβάλετο δὲ αὐτοὺς ὁ Φῆλιξ, ἀκριβέστερον εἰδὼς τὰ περὶ τῆς ὁδοῦ, εἴπας· Ὅταν Λυσίας ὁ χιλίαρχος καταβῇ διαγνώσομαι τὰ καθ’ ὑμᾶς·
records.gloss: Put off however them Felix, more accurately knowing the things concerning the Way, having said, When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide the things as to you;
pieces: Felix knew a good deal about the Way, and he postponed the matter. He told them, "I will rule on your case once Lysias the tribune comes down."

L.22: But Felix, knowing rather accurately the things concerning the Way, put them off, saying, "When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case."

R.22: Felix knew quite a lot about the Way. So he stopped the trial for the time being. He told them, "I will decide your case when Lysias comes down here." Lysias was the tribune who commanded the soldiers in Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: put them off: adjourned the hearing
decisions.reason: The verb is a legal term for postponing a case to a later date.

decisions.choice: knowing rather accurately: knowing more than the accusers supposed
decisions.reason: The comparative may mean that Felix knew more about the Way than the speeches had shown, or simply that he was well informed. His wife Drusilla was Jewish (24:24), and believers had lived in Judea for years. Either way, he saw that the case was weak.

decisions.choice: Lysias the tribune: the Roman commander of the garrison in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: A tribune commanded a cohort of about a thousand soldiers. Claudius Lysias had arrested Paul and sent him to Felix (21:31-33; 23:26-30). Luke does not say that he ever came.

decisions.choice: Lysias was the tribune who commanded the soldiers in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable explains the title in a sentence of its own.

decisions.choice: postponed the matter
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the plain legal sense of the verb.

records.source: διαταξάμενος τῷ ἑκατοντάρχῃ τηρεῖσθαι αὐτὸν ἔχειν τε ἄνεσιν καὶ μηδένα κωλύειν τῶν ἰδίων αὐτοῦ ὑπηρετεῖν αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: having ordered the centurion to keep him, to have then relief and no one to forbid of the own of him to serve him.
pieces: He gave orders to the centurion: Paul was to stay in custody, but with some relief from strict confinement, and none of his own people were to be kept from helping him.

L.23: He ordered the centurion that he be kept [in custody] and have some relief, and that he forbid none of his own [people] to serve him.

R.23: Felix told the centurion, an officer in charge of a hundred soldiers, to keep Paul under guard. But he told him to give Paul some freedom, and to let Paul's friends come and help him.

decisions.choice: the sentence goes on: Felix is still the one acting
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT marks a pause after 24:22, and the participle "having ordered" goes on telling what Felix did.

decisions.choice: relief: lighter custody, some freedom
decisions.reason: The word means a loosening. Paul stayed a prisoner but was not held in strict confinement (compare 28:16, 28:30).

decisions.choice: his own: his friends and companions
decisions.reason: The phrase means those who belonged to him. They could bring him food and other things he needed, as friends did for prisoners.

decisions.choice: the centurion: a Roman officer over about a hundred soldiers
decisions.reason: Centurions served under the tribune and guarded Paul on the way to Caesarea (23:23).

decisions.choice: a new sentence beginning "He" or "Felix"
decisions.reason: A participle cannot open an English sentence, so each level starts a new sentence and names the subject.

decisions.choice: Paul
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the prisoner.

decisions.choice: an officer in charge of a hundred soldiers
decisions.reason: Readable explains the title.

records.source: Μετὰ δὲ ἡμέρας τινὰς παραγενόμενος ὁ Φῆλιξ σὺν Δρουσίλλῃ τῇ ἰδίᾳ γυναικὶ οὔσῃ Ἰουδαίᾳ μετεπέμψατο τὸν Παῦλον καὶ ἤκουσεν αὐτοῦ περὶ τῆς εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν πίστεως.
records.gloss: After then days some having arrived Felix with Drusilla the own wife being a Jewess, he sent for Paul and heard him concerning the in Christ Jesus faith.
pieces: A few days afterward Felix arrived with Drusilla, his wife, a Jewish woman. He had Paul brought in and heard what he had to say about faith in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

L.24: And after some days Felix came with Drusilla his wife, who was a Jewess, and he sent for Paul and heard him concerning faith in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus.

R.24: A few days later, Felix came back with his wife Drusilla. She was Jewish. Felix sent for Paul and listened to him talk about having faith in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

decisions.choice: Drusilla: a Jewish princess, daughter of King Herod Agrippa I
decisions.reason: Drusilla was a daughter of the Herod who died in 12:20-23 and a sister of Agrippa and Bernice (25:13). Josephus says she left her first husband to marry Felix (Antiquities 20.141-143).

decisions.choice: having arrived: Felix came back, or came to the hearing room
alternatives: Felix arrived in Caesarea for the first time
decisions.reason: Luke does not say where Felix had been. The point is that he came with Drusilla and then sent for Paul.

decisions.choice: faith in Christ Jesus: trust directed to Jesus as the Messiah
decisions.reason: The preposition shows where the faith is directed, as in 20:21 and 26:18.

decisions.choice: having faith in
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the word faith and makes it an activity: trusting in Jesus.

records.heading: Felix and Drusilla hear Paul

records.source: διαλεγομένου δὲ αὐτοῦ περὶ δικαιοσύνης καὶ ἐγκρατείας καὶ τοῦ κρίματος τοῦ μέλλοντος ἔμφοβος γενόμενος ὁ Φῆλιξ ἀπεκρίθη· Τὸ νῦν ἔχον πορεύου, καιρὸν δὲ μεταλαβὼν μετακαλέσομαί σε·
records.gloss: Reasoning then him concerning righteousness and self-control and the judgment the coming, afraid having become Felix answered, The for now go, opportunity then having found I will summon you;
pieces: As Paul reasoned with him about righteousness, self-control and the judgment that is coming, Felix became alarmed. "Leave me for now," he answered. "I will call for you again when I find a suitable time."

L.25: And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix became afraid and answered, "Go for the present, and when I find an opportunity I will summon you."

R.25: Paul talked about righteousness, about controlling yourself, and about the day when God will judge everyone. Felix became afraid. He said, "Go away for now. When I have time, I will call for you again."

decisions.choice: righteousness: the right conduct that God requires
alternatives: God's gift of being made right with him
decisions.reason: Next to self-control and judgment, the word here means living justly, as God demands. Felix was known for injustice, and he had taken another man's wife.

decisions.choice: self-control: mastery over one's desires
decisions.reason: The word means command of oneself, especially over desires (Galatians 5:23).

decisions.choice: the coming judgment: God's judgment of all people
decisions.reason: Paul preached that God has fixed a day when he will judge the world (17:31).

decisions.choice: an opportunity: a convenient time
decisions.reason: The word means a fitting time. Felix puts Paul off until it suits him.

decisions.choice: the day when God will judge everyone
decisions.reason: Readable says whose judgment it is and whom it concerns, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: controlling yourself
decisions.reason: Readable uses a verb in place of an abstract noun.

records.source: ἅμα καὶ ἐλπίζων ὅτι χρήματα δοθήσεται αὐτῷ ὑπὸ τοῦ Παύλου· διὸ καὶ πυκνότερον αὐτὸν μεταπεμπόμενος ὡμίλει αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: At the same time also hoping that money will be given to him by Paul; therefore also more often him sending for he was conversing with him.
pieces: At the same time he hoped for money from Paul, so he had him brought in quite often and talked with him.

L.26: At the same time he was also hoping that money would be given to him by Paul; therefore he also sent for him rather often and conversed with him.

R.26: Felix also hoped that Paul would give him money to let him go free. So he often sent for Paul and talked with him.

decisions.choice: money: a bribe for Paul's release
decisions.reason: Roman law forbade governors to take money from those on trial, but the practice was common. Felix may have heard of the funds Paul had brought (24:17).

decisions.choice: rather often: quite frequently
decisions.reason: The comparative here means simply "fairly often".

decisions.choice: to let him go free
decisions.reason: Readable says what the money would be for, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: Διετίας δὲ πληρωθείσης ἔλαβεν διάδοχον ὁ Φῆλιξ Πόρκιον Φῆστον· θέλων τε χάριτα καταθέσθαι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις ὁ Φῆλιξ κατέλιπε τὸν Παῦλον δεδεμένον.
records.gloss: Two years however having been completed, received successor Felix Porcius Festus; wishing then favor to lay up with the Jews Felix left Paul bound.
pieces: Two full years went by, and then Porcius Festus succeeded Felix. Felix wished to earn the favor of the Jews, so he left Paul behind in chains.

L.27: But when two years had been completed, Felix received a successor, Porcius Festus; and wishing to gain favor with the Jews, Felix left Paul bound.

R.27: Two years later, a man named Porcius Festus took Felix's place as governor. Felix wanted to win the favor of the Jewish leaders, so he left Paul in prison.

decisions.choice: favor: goodwill from people, not the grace of God
decisions.reason: The word usually means God's grace, but here it is human goodwill, which Felix hoped to store up with the Jewish leaders (compare 25:3, 25:9). The same sense appears in 7:10 and 7:46.

decisions.choice: two years: the time Paul spent in custody in Caesarea
decisions.reason: The two years most naturally count Paul's imprisonment from 24:23. They are not the whole time Felix was governor.

decisions.choice: Porcius Festus: the next Roman governor of Judea
decisions.reason: Josephus tells that Felix was recalled to Rome after complaints from the Jews of Caesarea and that Festus took his place (Antiquities 20.182). Festus died in office after a short rule.

decisions.choice: to gain favor: to lay up goodwill for himself
alternatives: to do the Jews a kindness
decisions.reason: The verb means to deposit or store up. Felix wanted the Jewish leaders to owe him something as he left office.

decisions.choice: bound: in custody, a prisoner
decisions.reason: The word means bound, and Paul was in chains (26:29), though with some freedom (24:23).

decisions.choice: took Felix's place as governor
decisions.reason: Readable says what office Festus took.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Readable names the people whose goodwill Felix wanted: the leaders who had accused Paul.
